newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait wants foreigners to pay health insurance.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait wants foreigners to pay health insurance.

text.p: Kuwait plans to impose compulsory health insurance on its 1.2 million foreign residents to cut costs and what it sees as "excessive" use of health care services, a senior official said on Sunday.
"Medicine is expensive, so are medical equipment and technical staff," Abdul-Rahim al-Zaid, an undersecretary at the Gulf Arab state's Health Ministry, told Reuters.
The oil-rich state, with a total population of two million people, spends about 270 million dinars ($891 million) annually to provide health care virtually free of charge.
"We want to rationalise use of medical services."
Residents visit doctors at an average of eight times a year compared to an average of two visits in countries that impose fees, said Zaid.
Currently the state charges token fees on some medical services for expatriates, while nationals receive medical care free of charge, including treatment abroad for selected cases.
Kuwait, which produces some 2.0 million barrels of oil, is trying to eliminate its budget deficit by the year 2000 by reducing government spending and increasing non-oil income.
The 1.21 billion dinars shorfall forecast for the 1996/97 (July-June) budget makes about 13 percent of GDP according to private estimates.
The envisaged plan would oblige guest workers and their dependants to pay 50-70 dinars to insurance firms in addition to up to two dinars when they visit state health centres.
"We have a preliminary approval by the cabinet on the imposition of (obligatory) health insurance...We hope this plan would be implemented by 1998."
Such a measure requires the approval of parliament and the endorsement of the Emir Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah.
The plan would be managed by Kuwait's four insurance firms -- Al-Ahlia Insurance, Warba Insurance, Kuwait Insurance and Gulf Insurance.
"We, the ministry, will deal with national insurance firms" but those companies could involve foreign firms, said Zaid.
Diplomats and economists said the measure would not be popular with lower earners, people with a large number of dependants and foreign workers.
"I think the measure being obligatory would have a negative impact on foreign workers. It would be easier to impose fees on those who do not have insurance when they seek treatment," said a diplomat.
